newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Italy say determined to meet EMU deadline.
newsitem.headline: France, Italy say determined to meet EMU deadline.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Thursday they were determined their countries should join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on schedule in January 1999.
A French spokesman said Chirac telephoned Prodi to discuss economic and monetary questions and the future of NATO and European security arrangements.
"Each man reaffirmed his determination to see his country join the euro at the planned date," he said.

French sources said Chirac had above all sought to reassure Prodi in the half-hour conversation that France and Germany were not discussing any deal behind Rome's back to delay Italian membership of the planned single European currency.

In Rome, the Italian government described the talks as "long and cordial", following a series of tussles between France and Italy over nuclear testing, EMU and European security since Chirac took office in May 1995.

"The two examined the economic and monetary situation in Italy and in France with a prospect to both countries joining monetary union on the planned date of January 1, 1999," an Italian government statement said.

The centre-left Italian government has been ultra-sensitive at any suggestion that it might not qualify for the first wave of member countries, although economists doubt its chances of bringing its public sector deficit down to the required three percent of gross domestic product, from 6.8 percent last year.

Despite open reluctance in German banking circles, Paris and Bonn have stuck to the line that each country should do its best to meet the criteria for monetary union and a decision should be taken early next year on the basis of 1997 data.

Chirac angered Italy last year by saying it might not be ready to join the first wave of EMU. He has since said he is convinced that more countries than is widely assumed will be ready to join the single currency on January 1, 1999.

French officials privately say that if it became clear later this year that countries such as Italy and Spain would miss the criteria by a significant margin, creative diplomacy could be required to give them the prospect of joining in a second wave by the time euro banknotes and coins came into force in 2002.
Chirac's office said the two leaders also stressed the need for European Union countries to coordinate their economic policies to fight unemployment.
Paris is campaigning for an informal stability council of EMU member states to fulfil that role and serve as a political counterweight to the independent European Central Bank.

Chirac and Prodi also discussed the reform and enlargement of NATO, in which France is pressing the United States to yield the alliance's Naples-based Southern Command to a European, as well as wider European security issues.

Italy, which has refrained from backing France on the command issue, was angered last month when Chirac raised the idea of a "big five" summit to overcome Russia's opposition to NATO enlargement, excluding smaller NATO members.
The idea now appears to have been put aside in the face of opposition from the United States as well as the smaller allies and some East European candidates for NATO membership.
